newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin Wall mural restored by artists.
newsitem.headline: Berlin Wall mural restored by artists.

text.p: Work began on Sunday to restore the murals on a mile-long segment of the Berlin Wall, the longest piece left of the despised Cold War symbol of division.

The so-called East Side Gallery -- a 1.6 km-long piece of the wall that was transformed into a mosiac of murals by more than 100 artists in 1990 -- was falling into disrepair before badly needed touch-up work began on Sunday.

About fifteen of the original 118 painters from around the world who turned a stretch of the grey border into a collection of murals on the theme of the fall of the wall returned for the start of a ten-day effort to restore their work.

Known as the world's largest open air mural, the East Side Gallery near the main train station in east Berlin has been worn down by the elements and smeared with graffiti in the years since its creation in 1990.
The murals reflect the euphoria of the period immediately after the wall opened on November 9, 1989.
They show arms extending through the image of a crumbling wall for a hand-shake, East German Trabant cars driving through to West Berlin and scenes of the world peacefully uniting.

"It is especially important to save the wall now because in 30 or 40 years it will only be a memory," said artist Kani Alavi, who organised the restoration. "We want to use the wall to keep memories of this time alive for the next generation."
The international group of artists was unable to obtain any funding for the restoration work from the city of Berlin, which is struggling to close enormous budget deficits.
Many city officials want the wall -- which stands on a choice piece of land -- torn down.
A small ceremony at the start of the renovation work on Sunday was also marred when a vandal rushed towards artists Gerhardt and Anne Lahr and threw a can of red paint at the artists and their mural.
"I guess you always have to deal with such aggression," Anne Lahr said afterwards.
"For an outdoor gallery, it is normal that the work cannot really be protected," she added. "We will always have to return to restore this work because it is out here on an open street."
But at least one artist seemed not to mind the ravages of time.
Irena Dubrowskaya, one of four Muscovites who worked on the paintings in 1990, said she has enjoyed watching the city leave its mark on her work.
"This painting wasn't meant to last forever," she said.
